---
title: "Research"
---

My research asks how voters respond when climate shocks and energy infrastructure become politically visible, and what that means for accountability. I work with original geospatial data and causal inference designs, mostly in R.

## Working papers

::: {.paper-entry}
[Does Democracy Die in Darkness? Storm-Driven Blackouts, Turnout, and Vote Choice in São Paulo]{.paper-title}

- **Question.** Disasters reach voters less through wind and water than through the services that fail afterwards. When a windstorm cut power to millions of São Paulo residents between the two rounds of the 2024 mayoral election, did the blackout change how they voted?
- **Data.** An original outage dataset for the city's 104 electricity distribution areas, linked to geocoded election returns from 2008 to 2024.
- **Design.** Difference-in-differences with a continuous treatment and spatially robust inference; a two-way fixed-effects panel of mayoral runoffs; wind speed as an instrument for outage hours; rainfall and outages outside the storm window as placebos; randomization inference and entropy balancing.
- **Finding.** The incumbent's gain between rounds was about two points smaller in the hardest-hit quarter of the city. Turnout fell citywide, but local outages did not predict where.

Presented at ISA, MPSA, and the ISA–AMEI joint conference.
:::

::: {.paper-entry}
[Watt Drives Voters: The Politics of AI Data Center Energy Demand in Georgia's Public Service Commission Election]{.paper-title}

- **Question.** Georgia is one of ten U.S. states that elect their electricity regulators. As AI data centers drive up electricity demand, do voters hold those regulators accountable?
- **Data.** A county-level panel of data-center openings linked to election returns and survey data.
- **Design.** Synthetic control, synthetic difference-in-differences, and spatial spillover models.
:::

::: {.paper-entry}
[Decoupling Without Democracy: Does Economic Openness Drive Green Transitions in Authoritarian States?]{.paper-title}

- **Question.** Can trade openness push autocracies to decouple growth from emissions, absent electoral pressure?
- **Data.** A panel of 165 countries, 2001–2023.
- **Design.** Staggered difference-in-differences, synthetic control, and machine-learning screening of mechanisms.
:::

## Work in progress

**Disasters, blackouts, and voting in Japan.** Extending the São Paulo design to prolonged typhoon and earthquake blackouts in Japan, to ask whether voters blame utilities, local governments, or the governing parties.

## Methods

Difference-in-differences and event studies · synthetic control and synthetic DiD · instrumental variables · randomization inference · spatial econometrics and areal interpolation · statistical machine learning · expert surveys · R (fixest, sf, spdep, tidyverse)
